analysis.one_liner: Protects millions of acres of Northern Rockies federal land as wilderness, wild rivers, and wildlife corridors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in March 2019 and never advanced; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The Northern Rockies Ecosystem Protection Act would designate roughly 20 to 25 million acres of federal land in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness, add wild and scenic river protections, and connect those areas with biological corridors for wildlife. It would bar new road building, logging, mining, and oil and gas drilling in the protected lands, create restoration jobs rebuilding damaged acreage, and guarantee tribal rights to continue traditional uses of the protected areas. The bill's sponsors say the land is worth more as a source of clean water, fish and wildlife, and recreation than as subsidized logging and drilling ground.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be everyone who uses or values the Northern Rockies: hikers, hunters, anglers, and paddlers who keep access to wild public land, and downstream communities whose water comes from protected forest headwaters of the Columbia, Snake, Missouri, and other rivers. The bill also directs new spending to rural Mountain West communities, which would get federal contracts and outdoor-economy jobs doing restoration work on damaged land. Tribes would gain guaranteed access to protected areas for traditional cultural, spiritual, and subsistence uses. Taxpayers would also benefit modestly, because the bill ends below-cost timber sales that currently lose money when sold.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hunters, anglers, recreationists, Mountain West communities, tribes

how_it_helps.text: Designates millions of acres of federal land in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness — including large new wildernesses in Glacier, Yellowstone, and Grand Teton national parks and hundreds of named wilderness additions — permanently protecting them from development while leaving them open to the public for hunting, fishing, camping, and other non-motorized recreation.

Protects the headwaters of major river systems, including the Columbia, Snake, Green, and Missouri, and designates new wild and scenic rivers in Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming; the bill's findings state that protected roadless land produces clean water, protects native fisheries, and reduces water treatment and irrigation costs for farming, ranching, and municipal supplies.

Creates jobs and contracts for local businesses: the bill establishes wildland recovery areas and requires the Agriculture Department to write a recovery plan for each, directing restoration work on damaged land in rural Mountain West communities, which the findings say would employ people in outdoor trades and reduce taxpayer losses from below-cost timber sales.

Links the protected core ecosystems with designated biological connecting corridors so wide-ranging wildlife such as grizzly bears, wolves, lynx, and caribou can move and interbreed — a design conservation scientists consider necessary for species survival as the climate changes.

Protects tribal rights: the bill explicitly preserves Indian tribes' rights, treaty and otherwise, to use designated areas for traditional cultural, spiritual, and subsistence purposes, and applies the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act so tribes can take on roles in managing the protected land.

Prohibits new roads, logging, mining, and oil and gas development on the protected lands, and freezes development on un-designated roadless federal lands pending a study by a panel of independent scientists on their role in the region's biological diversity.

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on timber, mining, and oil and gas companies and their workers, who would lose access to the roadless federal lands the bill withdraws from logging, hardrock mining, and drilling, and on off-road vehicle users, who would be excluded from designated wilderness. Federal agencies would bear new management and restoration costs. Some local governments and rural communities dependent on timber revenue could lose a tax and employment base, though the bill's answer is publicly funded restoration and recreation work in the same communities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently bars road construction, timber harvest, mining, and oil and gas leasing across the designated lands, which would eliminate logging and extraction jobs and contract opportunities in some rural Mountain West communities that depend on that work, and would close designated areas to motorized recreation and new ski-resort development.

The bill imposes a top-down, Congressionally drawn reserve system covering five states, including hundreds of individually named wildernesses specified by acreage in statute; opponents and some locals argue such decisions should be reached through state or local collaboration rather than a single national mandate, and the bill's own findings acknowledge it aims to override what it calls unsatisfactory federal agency management of the region.

Federal agencies would take on the added cost of drafting recovery plans, running the interagency implementation team, and funding a multi-year scientific evaluation of the region's roadless lands, without a dedicated revenue source in the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — permanent protection of a largely intact wildland region that supplies clean water to major river systems and habitat for the only remaining populations south of Canada of caribou, gray wolves, and grizzly bears — is large and national, and the land would remain open to the public. The costs are real but concentrated: logging, mining, and drilling operators and their workers in specific rural communities would lose access to federal acreage, and agencies would take on new management duties. The bill attempts to offset the local economic loss with federally funded restoration jobs and by ending below-cost timber sales that currently lose taxpayer money. The main design criticism is its breadth: it imposes a single, congressionally dictated reserve map across five states rather than the negotiated local settlements that have produced most past wilderness laws, which is precisely why it has never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate bill was introduced and sent to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island introduced the Northern Rockies Ecosystem Protection Act in the Senate on March 14, 2019, joined by Senators Durbin, Menendez, Stabenow, and Markey.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources — the committee that controls public lands legislation.
That referral was the bill's last action. The committee never held a hearing, never voted on it, and the full Senate never debated it; the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress in January 2021.
A companion version was simultaneously championed in the House by Representative Carolyn Maloney, but no House passage occurred and no version of the bill became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber, mining, oil and gas, and motorized-recreation interests that would have lost access to protected federal land were better off: the bill died in committee without a vote, so no acreage was withdrawn and no extraction activity was restricted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber, mining, and drilling interests; unimpeded status quo

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its Senate sponsorship.

for.name: Sens. Durbin, Menendez, Stabenow, and Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 11 additional cosponsors (14 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors after introduction, bringing total Senate support to 15 of 100 senators — none from the five states whose land would be designated.

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the House companion (H.R. 1753) and championed the bill in the House.

for.name: Conservation organizations and the outdoor economy
for.what_they_did: Backed the bill as reflected in its findings on recreation, fisheries, and the restoration economy it would create.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Lisa Murkowski, R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in March 2019 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate committee calendar
against.what_they_did: Controlled the committee that never scheduled the bill, keeping it off the floor for the entire 116th Congress.

against.name: Timber, mining, and oil and gas industries
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed wilderness withdrawals of this scale in the Northern Rockies because the bill bars logging, mining, and drilling on the affected federal lands.

against.name: Western state delegations and motorized-recreation interests
against.what_they_did: Historically opposed this bill's large-scale top-down wilderness designations across Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Oregon, and Washington, including closing areas to motorized use and resource extraction.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 Senate cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent who caucuses with Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Senate committee never advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill prohibits timber harvest and new road construction across the designated roadless lands and ends below-cost timber sales, which the bill itself says lose taxpayer money. Logging operators and timber-dependent rural workers would lose access to federal supply.

industries.industry: Mining and oil and gas drilling
industries.note: The bill prohibits mineral, oil, and gas leasing and any development that would impair the roadless character of the protected lands, closing large federal acreage to future claims.

Wilderness and wild and scenic river designations preserve the scenery, fisheries, and wild land that outfitting, guiding, hunting, fishing, and tourism businesses rely on; the bill's findings say protecting the land draws new residents and businesses on quality of life.

industries.industry: Land restoration contractors and outdoor trades
industries.note: The bill creates wildland recovery areas where restoration work would be performed, generating federal contracts and employment for local businesses in rural Mountain West communities.

industries.industry: Ski resort and motorized recreation developers
industries.note: The bill's definition of development explicitly includes ski resort facilities, and wilderness designation excludes motorized vehicles, closing those options on the designated land.

industries.industry: Tribal nations of the Northern Rockies
industries.note: The bill preserves tribal treaty and traditional-use rights on the protected areas and opens the door to tribal management under the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act.
